a: bent down to peer into
p: Clement pictures study of Scripture as bending down to peer into something deep.
b: The Greek verb pictures someone bending low to look closely into a deep place. Clement uses it four times in this part of the letter: here of "the depths of the knowledge of God," then of the Corinthians, who "have bent down to look into the sacred Scriptures" (45:2), "the oracles of God" (53:1) and "the oracles of God's instruction" (62:3). The compliment has a point. People who have looked so closely into Scripture should know the order God gave, and should keep it.
orig: ἐγκεκυφότες (enkekyphotes), "having stooped to look into"

a: the offerings and the services
p: Two Temple words that later became church words: offering and liturgy.
b: Prosphora is an offering brought to God; the verb prospherō, "present," comes back in 41:2 and in 44:4, where the elders "presented the gifts." Leitourgia was the Greek word for a public duty done for a city, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the priests' work at the tent and the Temple (Numbers 4:24; 18:7 in the Greek). It is the word behind English "liturgy." Clement uses the same words for Israel's worship (40-41) and for the work of the church's overseers (44:2-6), and his argument depends on that bridge.
orig: τάς τε προσφορὰς καὶ λειτουργίας (tas te prosphoras kai leitourgias)

a: settled where he wants them carried out and by whom
p: The law fixed both the place of sacrifice and the people who offered it.
b: Clement sums up two rules of the law of Moses. The place: sacrifices are offered "only in the place the LORD will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:14; compare Deuteronomy 12:5-11), which for Clement is Jerusalem (41:2). The people: only Aaron's sons serve at the altar, with the Levites beside them (Numbers 3:5-10; 18:1-7). His point for Corinth comes in 42-44: God also settled who leads the church, through Christ and the apostles.

a: The layperson
p: Laikos, "of the people," here names the ordinary Israelite who is not a priest.
b: The adjective comes from laos, "people." Lightfoot notes that it is not found in the Septuagint, though the other Greek versions of the Old Testament use laikos for what is "laic" or "profane," that is, common rather than holy (on 40:5). Here it is the ordinary Israelite worshiper, set beside the high priest, the priests and the Levites. Later Christian writers used it, and the Latin laicus, for church members who are not clergy; Lightfoot cites Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian. The word is the root of English "lay" and "laity," though here Clement is still describing the Temple.
orig: ὁ λαϊκὸς ἄνθρωπος τοῖς λαϊκοῖς προστάγμασιν (ho laikos anthrōpos tois laikois prostagmasin)

a: For the high priest has been given his own services.
t: Does the Temple order stand for church offices?
p: Clement sets out four ranks of Israel's worship. Does he mean them as a pattern for church ranks?
b: Clement lists four ranks: high priest, priests, Levites, layperson. Then he turns to the church (41:1) and to the apostles' appointment of "overseers and deacons" (42:4). Do the ranks map one to one? Lightfoot, the Anglican editor of the letter, held that the letter "throughout only recognizes two orders, presbyters and deacons, as existing at Corinth" (on 40). On that reading Clement uses the Temple only to prove that God wants each person in his own place. The four ranks could also be taken as a model for a fixed Christian order of clergy and people, such as the church later built, but the text itself states the principle and leaves the mapping unsaid. For the churches' answers on priesthood, see the cards at Hebrews 7:23-28 and 1 Peter 2:5-9.

a: in his own rank
p: Tagma is a military word: a unit in its place in the battle line.
b: Tagma means a body of troops drawn up in order. Clement has already used army ranks as a picture of the church (37:3), and Paul uses the same word for the order of the resurrection: "each group has its own place in the order" (1 Corinthians 15:23). The rule of this verse, each one in his own rank, not stepping over the line of his service, sums up chapters 37-44. It is aimed at the Corinthians who had stepped out of their place and removed their elders (44:6).
orig: ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ τάγματι (en tō idiō tagmati)

a: They are presented in Jerusalem alone.
p: Clement speaks of the sacrifices in the present tense. Some have used this to date the letter before AD 70.
b: The verbs are present: the sacrifices "are presented" in Jerusalem. If the Temple was still standing, the letter would be earlier than its destruction by the Romans in AD 70. Lightfoot reports that this very early date "has been thought," but answers that "to this very early date however there are insuperable objections." He reads the present tense as speaking of the lasting record in the law, and notes that Josephus, writing his Antiquities about AD 93, and the Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 7) also describe the Temple rites in the present tense long after 70. Lake, for his part, dates the letter between 75 and 110 from chapters 5, 42 and 44, and does not use this verse.

a: the daily sacrifices
p: The Greek is "sacrifices of continuance": the lambs offered every morning and evening.
b: Clement's word endelechismos means "continuance." It stands for the Hebrew tamid, the regular burnt offering of two lambs a day (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8), which the Greek of Numbers 28:3 calls an offering made endelechōs, "continually." Clement then lists the sacrifices for vows (Leviticus 22:21) and for sin and for guilt (Leviticus 4-5). The list is a fair summary of the Temple's regular worship.
orig: θυσίαι ἐνδελεχισμοῦ (thysiai endelechismou)

a: checked the offering for any flaw
p: The law required a flawless animal. Clement says the priests checked it.
b: The Greek word means "inspected for a blemish." The law demanded it: an offering "must be flawless to be accepted. There must be no defect in it at all" (Leviticus 22:21; compare Malachi 1:8). The law does not itself say that the high priest inspected each animal; Clement describes the practice as he knew it or imagined it. His point is that even an animal had to pass a test before it reached the altar, just as the church's leaders were "tested" before they were appointed (42:4; 44:2).
orig: μωμοσκοπηθὲν (mōmoskopēthen)

a: have death as their penalty
t: Death for stepping out of place
p: The law threatened death to an outsider who came near the altar.
b: Clement has in mind laws like Numbers 18:7: "The outsider who comes near is to be put to death" (compare Numbers 1:51; 3:10). The story of Korah, who claimed the priesthood and went down alive into the earth, comes next (Numbers 16; 1 Clement 51:3-4). Clement does not threaten the Corinthians with death. He argues from the greater to the lesser: if breaking Israel's order was so serious, breaking the order Christ gave is no small thing (41:4; 44:4).

a: the more danger we stand in
p: Those who know more are judged more strictly, as Jesus said.
b: The rule matches the saying of Jesus: "When someone is given a lot, a lot will be looked for from him" (Luke 12:48). Clement includes himself ("we"). Christians know more than Israel did, because they know Christ, so breaking the church's order is a greater danger than breaking the Temple's. Hebrews argues the same way from the lesser to the greater (Hebrews 2:2-3; 10:28-29).

a: Jesus the Christ was sent out from God
p: God sent Christ, Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed overseers: the spine of chapters 42-44.
b: Clement builds a chain: God, Christ, the apostles (42:1-2), then the leaders the apostles appointed (42:4), then the men who took over from them (44:2). The first links come from the Gospels: "Just as the Father has sent me out, I too am sending you" (John 20:21; compare Matthew 10:40; Luke 10:16). The word "apostle" means "one sent." This chain, set out by a church writing within living memory of the apostles, is why the passage stands at the center of later arguments about succession from the apostles (see the deep section of 44 and the cards at Acts 1:20-26 and 2 Timothy 2:2).
r: John 20:21; John 17:18; Matthew 10:40; Luke 10:16; Acts 1:20-26; 2 Timothy 2:2

a: fully convinced by the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ
p: The apostles' certainty rests on the resurrection, the word of God and the Spirit.
b: The verb plērophoreō means "to be brought to full certainty." Clement names three grounds for the apostles' mission: the resurrection, the word of God, and "the full certainty the Holy Spirit gives." The same noun appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:5, where the good news came "with the Holy Spirit, and with a great certainty". The order matches Acts: the risen Jesus gives his orders (Acts 1:2-3), and the Spirit comes before they go out (Acts 1:8; 2:1-4).
orig: πληροφορηθέντες (plērophorēthentes)

a: their firstfruits
p: The first converts in each place, like the first of the harvest given to God.
b: The "firstfruits" were the first part of the harvest, given to God (Leviticus 23:10). Paul uses the word for the first believers in a region: "the household of Stephanas was the firstfruits of Achaia, and ... they have devoted themselves to serving the saints" (1 Corinthians 16:15; compare Romans 16:5). Achaia is the province of Corinth, so Clement's readers may have thought of that very household. Clement says the apostles appointed such first converts, after testing them.
orig: τὰς ἀπαρχὰς αὐτῶν (tas aparchas autōn)

a: overseers and deacons
p: Clement names two church offices, overseers and deacons. Are the overseers the same men as the elders?
b: Clement names only two offices, "overseers and deacons," the same pair as Philippians 1:1. In 44:4-5 he passes from those "out of the office of overseer" straight to "the elders," as if they were one group, and in 57:1 and 54:2 he tells the rebels to submit to "the elders." Lightfoot concluded that "episkopos and presbyteros therefore are synonymes in Clement, as they are in the Apostolic writers" (on 42:4). Lake, too, speaks of the deposed men as "Presbyters." Whether bishops are a separate order above the elders, and how early that order came, the churches answer differently: see the cards at Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1:5-7.
r: Philippians 1:1; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; 1 Timothy 3:1-13; Titus 1:5-7; 1 Peter 5:1-2

a: by the Spirit
p: The apostles tested their appointees, as 1 Timothy requires of deacons.
b: The verb is the one in 1 Timothy 3:10: "These also should be tested first. Then let them serve." Clement adds "by the Spirit," which may mean through prophecy, as when the Spirit named Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2), or through spiritual discernment. The same word marks the men who were to take over later, "other tested men" (44:2), and Apollos, "a man those apostles had tested" (47:4).

a: I will appoint their overseers in righteousness and their deacons in faith.
p: Clement's "Scripture" is Isaiah 60:17 in the Greek, reshaped to name overseers and deacons.
b: The Hebrew of Isaiah 60:17 reads, in the site's wording, "I will make peace your governor and righteousness your taskmaster." The Greek translation turned this into "I will give your rulers in peace and your overseers (episkopous) in righteousness" (Swete). Clement keeps "overseers in righteousness" but replaces the rulers with "deacons in faith." Lightfoot calls it "loosely quoted from LXX Is. lx. 17" and says that "the introduction of the diakonoi is due to misquotation." He notes that Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.26.5) also applies the verse to church leaders but quotes the Greek correctly. Whether Clement misremembered the verse or reshaped it on purpose, he does not say; either way, the prophecy of a peaceful, righteous Zion becomes a promise of church leaders.
orig: Καταστήσω τοὺς ἐπισκόπους αὐτῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ τοὺς διακόνους αὐτῶν ἐν πίστει

a: "a faithful attendant in the whole house,"
p: Numbers 12:7 in the Greek, the same verse Hebrews 3 uses for Moses.
b: The words come from God's praise of Moses in Numbers 12:7, where the Greek calls Moses a therapōn, an "attendant" or trusted servant, faithful "in my whole house." Hebrews uses the same verse: "Moses was faithful in the whole of God's house as an attendant" (Hebrews 3:5). Clement calls Moses God's "attendant" again in 51:3, 51:5 and 53:5. He gives Moses the title here because the next story shows Moses putting an end to a quarrel over who should serve.
orig: ὁ μακάριος πιστὸς θεράπων ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ (ho makarios pistos therapōn en holō tō oikō)

a: Jealousy once broke out over the priesthood
p: Clement retells Numbers 17 with details the Bible does not have: the seals, the keys and the table.
b: In Numbers 17, after Korah's revolt, each tribe's leader brings a staff, Moses lays them "in the tent of meeting in front of the testimony," and the next day Aaron's staff has "brought out buds, burst into blossom and ripened almonds" (Numbers 17:4, 8). Clement adds that the rods were tied together and sealed with the leaders' rings, that the tent's keys were sealed, that all Israel, the "six hundred thousand men" (compare Exodus 12:37), was called together, and that the rods lay "on God's table." None of these details is in Numbers. Whether Clement took them from a Jewish retelling or added them himself to show that no one could cheat, his point is plain: God settled the dispute, so that no one could argue with the result.

a: Did Moses not know ahead of time that this would happen?
t: Why the test, if Moses knew?
p: Moses knew the answer and held the test anyway, to stop disorder. Clement says the apostles did the same.
b: Clement's question sets up the next chapter. Moses already knew God had chosen Aaron, yet he staged a public test so that "there would be no disorder in Israel." In the same way "our apostles also knew" ahead of time that the office of overseer would be fought over, and they made provision (44:1-2). The parallel shows how Clement reads the Old Testament: as a set of examples whose purpose is the peace of God's people (compare 1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). The word for "disorder," akatastasia, is the one Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 14:33: God is not a God of disorder.

a: the title of overseer would be fought over
p: Clement says the apostles foresaw quarrels over the office. Paul warned the Ephesian elders the same way.
b: Literally "there would be fighting over the name of the office of overseer." Clement says the apostles knew this "through our Lord Jesus Christ," which may mean by revelation or by Jesus' own warnings about rivalry among his followers (Mark 10:42-44). Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus is the nearest parallel: "out of your own group men will stand up and say twisted things, so they can pull the disciples away to follow them" (Acts 20:30). The word "fighting" (eris) is the same as in 1 Corinthians 1:11, where Paul hears of "quarrels" at Corinth.
orig: ἔρις ἔσται ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀνόματος τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς (eris estai epi tou onomatos tēs episkopēs)

a: if they fell asleep
p: If "they" fell asleep: the men the apostles appointed (Lightfoot), or the apostles themselves (Rothe)?
b: The Greek says only "if they fall asleep" (die), with no subject named. Lightfoot takes "they" to be "the first generation of presbyters appointed by the Apostles themselves": when those overseers died, other tested men would take over their service. Rothe, as Lightfoot reports him, referred "they" to the apostles themselves and read the verse as founding the office of bishop; Lightfoot answers that this "interrupts the context with irrelevant matter." The first reading describes a rule for filling the local office; the second comes closer to a succession from the apostles. Lake's English ("if they should fall asleep, other approved men should succeed to their ministry") keeps the ambiguity, and so does the Plain English Translation. The Catholic Catechism paraphrases the verse as a ruling "that likewise on their death other proven men should take over their ministry" (CCC 861, citing chapters 42 and 44).

a: with the whole church agreeing
p: Later leaders were appointed by respected men "with the whole church agreeing." Who chose them?
b: Clement names three parties: the apostles, "other respected men" who appointed later leaders, and "the whole church," which agreed. The verb means "joining in approval"; it does not say how the church gave its approval. Lightfoot, following the older editor Wotton, compares Cyprian's phrase plebis suffragium, "the vote of the people," for the people's part in appointing church officers in the 200s. Acts has both: the apostles ask the believers to pick the Seven, then lay hands on them (Acts 6:3-6), and Paul and Barnabas "chose elders" in each church (Acts 14:23). The churches' answers to who should choose a church's ministers are on the card at Acts 14:23. Here Clement's point is that these men were appointed properly and have served well, so their removal was wrong.
orig: συνευδοκησάσης τῆς ἐκκλησίας πάσης (syneudokēsasēs tēs ekklēsias pasēs)

a: with no vulgar self-seeking
p: A rare word: Lake has "disinterestedly," Lightfoot "unassumingly."
b: Abanausōs is "not in a banausos way." Lake translates "disinterestedly": the elders sought nothing for themselves. Lightfoot translates "unassumingly" and explains the sense as the opposite of "vulgar self-assertion," noting that in Aristotle's Ethics banausia is vulgar, showy excess. The Plain English Translation's "with no vulgar self-seeking" tries to hold both: no grasping for gain, no pushing oneself forward. Lightfoot points to the same root in 49:5, "There is nothing vulgar in love, nothing arrogant," where it again stands beside pride. The lists for overseers and deacons ask the same: "free from the love of money" (1 Timothy 3:3), "not greedy for shameful profit" (Titus 1:7; compare 1 Timothy 3:8; 1 Peter 5:2).
orig: ἀβαναύσως (abanausōs)

a: presented the gifts
t: What gifts did the elders present?
p: The overseers "presented the gifts." Prayers, alms, the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, or all of these?
b: In the Greek, "of the office of overseer" belongs to "the gifts": the elders "presented the gifts of the office of overseer," the offerings that belong to that office. The phrase uses the Temple word for bringing an offering to the altar (40:2; 41:2; compare Matthew 5:23-24, "presenting your offering," and Hebrews 5:1, where a high priest is put in place "to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins"). Clement does not say what the gifts are. Lightfoot answered: "the prayers and thanksgivings, the alms, the eucharistic elements, the contributions to the agape," which the elders presented to God in the name of the church. Those who see the Lord's Supper as a sacrifice read here an early witness to the clergy offering the Eucharist; those who do not read the gifts as prayers and offerings of the people. Whether the Lord's Supper is a sacrifice is the card at Malachi 1:11, Luke 22:19 and Psalm 40.
orig: προσενεγκόντας τὰ δῶρα τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς (prosenenkontas ta dōra tēs episkopēs)

a: Blessed are the elders
p: In one breath Clement moves from the office of overseer (44:4) to "the elders" (44:5).
b: The removed men held "the office of overseer" (44:4), and in the next sentence the faithful men who have died are "elders." The same switch happens in Acts 20:17, 28 and Titus 1:5-7, where the elders are called overseers. The Plain English Translation keeps "overseer" for episkopos and "elder" for presbyteros everywhere, so the reader can see both words and judge whether they name one office (see the note at 42:4). Presbyteros also means simply "older man," which may be its sense in 1:3 and 21:6; here the office is meant, since these men held the "place set up for them."
orig: μακάριοι οἱ προοδοιπορήσαντες πρεσβύτεροι (makarioi hoi prohodoiporēsantes presbyteroi)

a: you have moved some men out of the service
p: This verse is the plainest statement of the trouble: blameless elders had been removed.
b: Here at last Clement says what the whole letter is about. The Corinthians "have moved some men out of the service," though they served "without blame" and lived well. Lake sums up the letter as written "in consequence of trouble in the latter community which had led to the deposition of certain Presbyters." Clement gives no charge against the men, no names, and no reason for the removal, except jealousy (3:2; 63:2) and "one or two people" behind it (47:6). He calls for the leaders of the revolt to leave (54:2) and to submit to the elders (57:1), which suggests the removed elders could be restored.

a: You love a quarrel, brothers
p: The Greek can be a statement or a command, and it can be irony.
b: The verb "you are" (este) has the same form as the command "be." So the sentence may say "You love a quarrel and are zealous for salvation" (a statement, perhaps ironic), or "Be quarrelsome, brothers, and zealous, over the things that lead to salvation" (a command: fight, if you must, about what matters). Lake reads it as a statement. Either way Clement turns the Corinthians' fighting spirit toward something worth zeal, and then appeals to the Scriptures they know so well (45:2).
orig: Φιλόνεικοι ἔστε, ἀδελφοί, καὶ ζηλωταί (Philoneikoi este, adelphoi, kai zēlōtai)

a: the ones given through the Holy Spirit
p: For Clement "the sacred Scriptures" are true, given through the Holy Spirit and free of anything unjust.
b: Clement says three things about "the sacred Scriptures": they are true, they were given "through the Holy Spirit," and "nothing unjust or falsified is written in them" (45:3). The New Testament says the same of the Old Testament (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). By "Scriptures" Clement means the Greek Old Testament, which he quotes on almost every page. He treats Paul's letter as written "truly led by the Spirit" (47:3), and he says his own letter was written "through the Holy Spirit" (63:2), but he never calls either "Scripture." His wording here agrees with the 66 books' own claims; the question of which books belong is on the cards at 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:20.

a: They were stoned by lawbreakers.
p: Clement's list follows the roll of sufferers in Hebrews 11.
b: The sequence of hunted, imprisoned, stoned and killed echoes Hebrews 11:36-37: "They were stoned. They were sawed in two. They died by murder with the sword." Jesus also called Jerusalem the "stoner of those sent to her" (Matthew 23:37). Clement's point is new: in every case the persecutors were wicked, never "holy men" (45:3). So when the Corinthians remove blameless elders, they stand on the wrong side of the story.

a: Was Daniel thrown into the lions' pit
p: The two great rescues of Daniel, chosen because the persecutors were enemies of God.
b: Clement takes his examples from Daniel 6 (Daniel among the lions: "they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions' den," Daniel 6:16) and Daniel 3 (the three young men in the furnace). Hebrews 11:33-34 joins the same two stories: they "shut lions' mouths, put out the power of fire." Clement uses the Greek word lakkos, "pit," as the Greek Daniel does. In both stories, his point runs, the attackers were idol-worshipers and schemers, not people who feared God.

a: Ananias, Azarias and Misael
p: These are the Hebrew names of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, in their Greek forms.
b: Daniel 1:6-7 gives the three friends' Hebrew names, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, and the Babylonian names, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Clement uses the Hebrew names in Greek form, as the Greek Daniel does in the song the three sing in the furnace ("Ananias, Azarias, Misael, bless the Lord," Daniel 3:88 in Theodotion's Greek, part of the Additions to Daniel). His order, Ananias, Azarias, Misael, is the order of that song.
orig: Ἀνανίας καὶ Ἀζαρίας καὶ Μισαήλ (Ananias kai Azarias kai Misaēl)

a: the champion and shield
p: Two Greek Psalm words for God as the defender of those who trust him.
b: Hypermachos is one who fights on another's behalf, a champion. Hyperaspistēs is one who holds a shield over another; the Greek Psalms use it for God: "my shield-bearer and horn of salvation" (Psalm 18:2, Greek 17:3) and "a shield-bearer of all who hope in him" (Psalm 18:30, Greek 17:31). The site's Psalm 18:2, made from the Hebrew, has "my shield and the horn that saves me."
orig: ὑπέρμαχος καὶ ὑπερασπιστής (hypermachos kai hyperaspistēs)

a: God wrote their names
p: Those who endured are written into God's record of remembrance.
b: The Greek says they "became enrolled by God in his memorial." The picture is God's book of remembrance: "a scroll of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the LORD" (Malachi 3:16), and the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5). Codex Alexandrinus reads "in their memorial" (see the variant).

a: "Cling to the holy, because those who cling to them will be made holy."
p: Clement says "it is written," but no known book has these words.
b: Clement introduces the saying with "it is written," his usual formula for Scripture, but no book of the Old Testament, in Hebrew or Greek, has it in this form. Lightfoot: "This quotation is no where found in the Old Testament." He names the nearest words, Sirach 6:34 ("Is someone wise? Hold tight to him"), and similar phrases in the Shepherd of Hermas (Visions 3.6; Similitudes 8.8 and 9.20: those who do not "cling to the saints" or "to the servants of God"). He suggests it is "perhaps another of those apocryphal quotations" found elsewhere in the letter, "or possibly Clement is giving from memory the sense of some canonical text or texts." Other unknown "Scriptures" in the letter stand at 17:6 and 23:3-4. Clement of Alexandria repeats the saying with "it is written" (Lightfoot, citing Stromata 5).

a: "With an innocent man you will be innocent
p: Clement quotes the Greek Psalm, shortened, and the Greek differs from the Hebrew.
b: The words are Psalm 18:25-26 in the Greek (Psalm 17:26-27 there), shortened. Swete's Greek begins "with the holy you will be made holy" (meta hosiou hosiōthēsē), and Clement leaves that line out, starting at "with an innocent man." The line he drops sounds much like the saying he has just quoted in 46:2, "those who cling to them will be made holy." The Hebrew, in the site's wording, says to God: "with the wholehearted man you show yourself wholehearted ... but with the twisted you twist and turn" (Psalm 18:25-26). In the Hebrew the psalm describes how God deals with each kind of person. The Greek can be read as describing how a person becomes like the company he keeps, and Clement reads it that way: cling to the innocent and you will be innocent.

a: fights and outbursts of anger and divisions and splits
p: Clement's list of the Corinthians' faults borrows Paul's words.
b: Three of these words stand in Paul's list of "the works of the flesh": "fighting, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambition, splits, factions" (Galatians 5:20). The site's Galatians uses "splits" for dichostasiai; this letter keeps "split" for schisma, Paul's word for the divisions at Corinth ("let there be no divisions among you," 1 Corinthians 1:10), and "division" for dichostasia. "War" is Clement's own strong word for a church quarrel (compare James 4:1).
orig: ἔρεις καὶ θυμοὶ καὶ διχοστασίαι καὶ σχίσματα πόλεμός τε (ereis kai thymoi kai dichostasiai kai schismata polemos te)

a: one Spirit of grace poured out on us
t: One God, one Christ, one Spirit
p: Clement's appeal to unity is close to Ephesians 4:4-6.
b: Clement names one God, one Christ, one Spirit, one calling, much as Ephesians 4:4-6 does: "There is one body and one Spirit. In the same way, you were called into one hope, the hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all." "Spirit of grace" is the phrase of Hebrews 10:29 and Zechariah 12:10, and "poured out" recalls Acts 2:17 and Titus 3:6. The triad of God, Christ and Spirit returns in Clement's oath at 58:2.

a: we are members of one another
p: Paul's picture of the church as one body, from his letters to Rome and to Corinth.
b: Clement writes from Rome to Corinth, and he uses the picture Paul gave to both: "we are one body in Christ, and each of us is a part belonging to the others" (Romans 12:5), and "you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a part of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27). He has already used the body as a picture of the church (37:5-38:1). Now the Corinthians are tearing it apart. The verb "rebel" (stasiazō) belongs to the word Clement uses for the whole revolt, stasis, "rebellion."

a: Woe to that man!
t: A saying of Jesus, in Clement's form
p: Clement joins two sayings of Jesus that the Gospels keep apart.
b: Clement's saying joins two Gospel sayings. The first is about Judas: "woe to the man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! Better for that man never to have been born" (Matthew 26:24; Mark 14:21). The second is about leading others astray: "He would be better off if a millstone were put around his neck and he were hurled into the sea, than that he should trip up one of these little ones" (Luke 17:2; compare Matthew 18:6; Mark 9:42). Clement's wording matches none of the Gospels exactly, and he has "my chosen" where the Gospels have "little ones" (see the variant). Whether he knew written Gospels or sayings passed on by mouth is argued. Compare the "words of the Lord Jesus" at 13:1-2.

a: Take up the letter of the blessed Paul the apostle.
p: Clement sends the Corinthians back to Paul's letter, which they still had.
b: Clement expects the Corinthians to have Paul's letter in hand and to read it again. What he says next, that Paul wrote "about himself and Cephas and Apollos, because even then you had taken sides" (47:3), matches 1 Corinthians 1:12 ("Each of you is saying, 'I belong to Paul,' or 'I belong to Apollos,' or 'I belong to Cephas'") and 3:4-6. So this is our 1 Corinthians, named and used by another church some decades later. Clement speaks of "the letter," singular, though Paul wrote more than once to Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:9; 2 Corinthians). He quotes or echoes 1 Corinthians often (37-38; 48:5; 49:5).

a: at the start of the gospel
p: The early days of the preaching in a place, as Philippians 4:15.
b: Lightfoot explains the phrase as "in the first days of the Gospel, soon after your conversion," when Paul first preached in Corinth and wrote to them. Paul uses the same phrase to the Philippians: "in the early days of the good news" (Philippians 4:15). Lightfoot takes "first" ("What did he write to you first") as "first and foremost," the prominence the topic has in 1 Corinthians, where the party slogans come in chapter 1. Either way, the point is the same: even in the first years the Corinthians took sides.
orig: ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (en archē tou euangeliou)

a: He was truly led by the Spirit when he wrote
p: Clement says Paul wrote "in truth, spiritually." How high is that claim?
b: The Greek is "in truth, spiritually he wrote to you." Clement treats Paul's letter as carrying the Spirit's guidance, as Paul himself claimed: "I think I also have God's Spirit" (1 Corinthians 7:40; compare 1 Corinthians 14:37). Clement does not call it "Scripture" or introduce it with "it is written," the formula he keeps for the Old Testament (46:2; 50:4). He claims the Spirit for his own letter too, in different words: it was written "through the Holy Spirit" (63:2).
orig: ἐπ᾽ ἀληθείας πνευματικῶς ἐπέστειλεν ὑμῖν (ep' alētheias pneumatikōs epesteilen hymin)

a: a man those apostles had tested
p: Clement calls Paul and Cephas apostles, and Apollos a man they had tested.
b: Clement ranks the three. Paul and Cephas (Peter) are "apostles who had a good name." Apollos is not an apostle but "a man those apostles had tested," as Acts describes him: an eloquent Jew from Alexandria whom Priscilla and Aquila taught more exactly, and whom the believers sent on to Achaia with a letter (Acts 18:24-28). The old factions had at least followed worthy leaders. The new one follows "one or two people" (47:6).

a: because of one or two people
p: The revolt was led by very few, though the whole church went along.
b: Clement blames the trouble on "one or two people," literally "one or two faces," elsewhere on a few rash and self-willed persons, as Lake's English of 1:1 puts it, and "the leaders of the rebellion" (51:1). Yet he addresses the whole church, which has "moved" the elders (44:6). The small number may be real, or it may be Clement's way of making the rebels look like a tiny faction against "the solid and ancient church." It is the only clue in the letter to the size of the group.

a: people who do not share our faith
p: Outsiders who are not Christians, who now speak ill of the church.
b: Heteroklineis means "leaning the other way." Lake translates "those who dissent from us." The word points to outsiders, non-Christians who now hear of the quarrel; Lightfoot compares the same word in 11:1 and in Epictetus. The worry is old: "The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you" (Romans 2:24, quoting Isaiah 52:5), and the household codes ask believers to live so that "the word of God" is not insulted (Titus 2:5; 1 Timothy 6:1).
orig: εἰς τοὺς ἑτεροκλινεῖς ὑπάρχοντας ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν (eis tous heteroklineis hyparchontas aph' hēmōn)

a: Open the gates of righteousness for me
p: Psalm 118:19-20 in the Greek. Clement reads the "gate" as Christ.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 118:19-20 (Greek 117:19-20). The site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, reads "Open the gates of righteousness for me; I will enter them and give Yah thanks. This is the gate that belongs to the LORD; through it the righteous will enter." Clement's Greek has "Lord" for the divine name and, in some witnesses, "so that I may ... give thanks" (see the variant). The verb, exomologeomai, means both "confess" and "give thanks, praise"; Clement plays on that range in 52:1-2. In 48:4 he makes the gate of righteousness "the one in Christ," as Jesus called himself the door (John 10:9).

a: Many gates stand open
p: Does Clement mean other ways to God, or many open doors of virtue, one of which is Christ's?
b: Clement says "many gates" are open but the gate "in righteousness" is "the one in Christ." Lightfoot suggests "perhaps a reference to our Lord's saying" about the narrow gate and the wide one (Matthew 7:13-14), and for the one gate in Christ points to John 10:9 and the Shepherd of Hermas. The next verse (48:5) also allows another sense: the many gates could be the many gifts it lists (faith, knowledge, wisdom, purity), all of which must lead through the one gate of Christ. The line "holiness and righteousness" echoes Zechariah's song: "in holiness and righteousness in his presence" (Luke 1:75).

a: Let a man be faithful.
p: Faith, knowledge and wisdom are good. The more gifted a man seems, the humbler he should be.
b: The four "let him be" lines list gifts the Corinthians prized: faith, the gift of speaking knowledge, wisdom in judging what is said, purity of life. Paul's list is close: "a message of wisdom ... a message of knowledge ... faith" (1 Corinthians 12:8-9), and he too warned that knowledge puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1). Clement grants every gift and then turns it (48:6): greatness should make a man humbler and more concerned for what benefits everyone, Paul's own rule (1 Corinthians 10:24, 33). The rebels at Corinth may have claimed such gifts.

a: Love lays a cover over a great number of sins.
p: Clement's praise of love follows 1 Corinthians 13 and quotes 1 Peter 4:8.
b: This chapter is Clement's own song of love, written to the church that first heard 1 Corinthians 13. The line "Love lays a cover over a great number of sins" is the site's 1 Peter 4:8 word for word (compare Proverbs 10:12, "love lays a cover over all wrongdoing," and James 5:20). Paul's "It covers all things" and "Love is slow to anger" (1 Corinthians 13:4, 7) stand behind "Love puts up with everything and is patient in everything," though Clement uses a different verb for the first. Then Clement adds his own lines, aimed at Corinth: "Love has no split. Love does not rebel. Love does everything in harmony."

a: his flesh for our flesh, and his soul for our souls
p: An early statement outside the New Testament of Christ giving each part of himself for us.
b: Clement says Jesus gave "his blood for us," and then pairs each part: his flesh for our flesh, his soul for our souls. The Greek hyper, "on behalf of," is the word of the Last Supper and of Paul (Luke 22:19-20; Galatians 1:4; John 10:11, 15). The pairing can be taken as exchange, Christ in our place part for part, or more widely, "on behalf of," as Christ giving every part of himself for every part of us; the verse does not explain how the gift works. The site's topic on the atonement sets out the views and who holds them.
orig: τὴν σάρκα ὑπὲρ τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν (tēn sarka hyper tēs sarkos hēmōn kai tēn psychēn hyper tōn psychōn hēmōn)

a: comes to visit
p: Episkopē means both the office of overseer (44:1) and God's coming visit.
b: The noun here is episkopē, the word translated "the office of overseer" in 44:4. Its root meaning is "looking over," and in the Greek Bible it often means the time God comes to look into things, to save or to judge (Luke 19:44; 1 Peter 2:12). Here it is the coming of Christ's kingdom, when those made perfect in love "will be shown openly." English cannot keep one word for both senses, but Clement's Greek readers would hear the link: the overseers watch over the flock until God himself comes to watch over all.
orig: ἐν τῇ ἐπισκοπῇ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ (en tē episkopē tēs basileias tou Christou)

a: Go into your inner rooms for a very little while
p: Clement joins Isaiah 26:20 and Ezekiel 37:12 into one "it is written."
b: The first half is Isaiah 26:20 in the Greek ("enter into your inner rooms ... hide for a very little while, until the anger of the Lord passes by"). The site's Isaiah, from the Hebrew, reads "go into your inner rooms and close your door after you. Hide for just a moment until the fury goes past." The last line comes from Ezekiel 37:12: "I will lift you out of your graves, my people." "I will remember a good day" is in neither and may be Clement's bridge. Joined, the verses promise the dead in love a resurrection, which fits the verse just before in Isaiah, 26:19, "Your dead will live."

a: if we have been doing
p: The verb is past ("were doing"), where the sense wants a present. Lake thinks the text is corrupt.
b: The Greek verb is imperfect, "we were doing." Lake notes: "This seems corrupt: a present is required." Lightfoot explains how the past could stand: "If the reading be correct, the point of time denoted in esmen ["we are"] must be the second advent, so that the deeds of this present life are regarded as past." The Plain English Translation keeps a past form of the verb, "have been doing," rather than change it to a present, since Lake reports no manuscript that reads otherwise. The sense is clear either way: we are blessed if we keep God's commands in love, so that our sins are forgiven.
orig: ἐποιοῦμεν (epoioumen), "we were doing"

a: Blessed are those whose lawless acts have been forgiven
p: Clement quotes Psalm 32:1-2 in the Greek, the same words Paul quotes in Romans 4:7-8.
b: Clement's first three lines are word for word the Greek Psalm 32:1-2 (31:1-2 there), which Paul also quotes, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's Romans 4:7-8: "Blessed are those whose lawless acts have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered over. Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never reckon." Clement goes on with the psalm's next line, "and in whose mouth there is no deceit," which Paul does not quote (the site's Psalm 32:2 from the Hebrew: "whose spirit holds no trickery"). Paul uses the psalm for righteousness by faith apart from works; Clement uses it for forgiveness that comes "through love" (50:5). Both say forgiveness is God's gift.

a: the enemy
p: "The one who opposes" is the devil, behind the Corinthian revolt.
b: Ho antikeimenos, "the one lying against," is a name for the devil, as in 1 Timothy 5:14 ("hand the opponent no opening for abuse"). Clement does not blame the devil to excuse the rebels. He includes himself and the Romans ("we have slipped"), and he asks that the wrong be forgiven. Then he turns to "the leaders of the rebellion." On the reading of this phrase see the variant.
orig: διά τινας παρεμπτώσεις τοῦ ἀντικειμένου (dia tinas paremptōseis tou antikeimenou)

a: the way the hearts of those who rebelled against God's attendant Moses were hardened
p: The rebels against Moses in Numbers 16 are Clement's warning to the rebels at Corinth.
b: Korah, Dathan and Abiram led a revolt against Moses and Aaron, claiming that the whole community was holy and asking why Moses set himself over them (Numbers 16:3). The earth opened and swallowed them: "They and all that was theirs went down alive to Sheol" (Numbers 16:33). Clement quotes the Greek of that verse ("they went down alive into Hades," 51:4) and joins it to Psalm 49:14: "Death will be their shepherd." Jude 11 uses the same story against troublemakers. For Clement it fits exactly: a revolt against God-given leaders.

a: were sunk in the Red Sea and died
p: Pharaoh's army is the second example of hearts hardened against God's signs.
b: Clement echoes Exodus 14:23 and 15:4: Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen went into the sea. His reason for their death is the "hardening" of their hearts after the signs and wonders, which Exodus tells again and again (Exodus 7:13; 14:4, 17). The lesson for Corinth: it is better to confess than to harden one's heart (51:3). See the topic on hardening of the heart.

a: the Master of all things needs nothing
p: God does not need sacrifices. What he asks is confession.
b: The Greek word means "without need." Paul said the same to the Athenians: "Nor do human hands tend to him, as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25), and Psalm 50:9-13 has God say he needs no bull from anyone's farm. Clement then gives what God does ask: exomologeisthai, which means to confess sins and also to give thanks and praise. In 52:2 David says "I will confess to the Lord." The single Greek word holds both, and Clement means both: an honest confession that is also praise.

a: it will please him more than a young calf that is growing horns and hoofs
p: Clement's David verse is Psalm 69:30-32, with the Greek's "calf" and "poor."
b: The words are close to Psalm 69:31-32 in the Greek (68:32-33 there): "it will please God more than a young calf putting out horns and hoofs. Let the poor see and be glad." The site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, reads "The LORD will like that better than an ox, than a young bull with horns and hooves. The humble see it and are glad" (Psalm 69:31-32). Clement's first line, "I will confess to the Lord," is his own form of the psalm's opening, where the Greek has "I will praise" (Psalm 69:30). Clement calls David "the chosen one," as Psalm 89:3 does.

a: Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise
p: Two more psalms in the Greek: the sacrifice of praise and the broken spirit.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 50:14-15 in the Greek (49:14-15 there), which has "a sacrifice of praise" where the site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, has "Sacrifice a thank offering to God" (Psalm 50:14). Hebrews uses the Greek phrase: "let us keep bringing up to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name" (Hebrews 13:15). Then he adds Psalm 51:17, in the site's wording "A broken spirit: that is the sacrifice for God." Clement has already quoted Psalm 51 in full (18:2-17).

a: the oracles of God
p: Ta logia, "the sayings," a name for Scripture as God's spoken words.
b: Ta logia tou theou is Paul's phrase in Romans 3:2: the Jews "were put in charge of the oracles of God." It means God's spoken words, here the Scriptures. Clement repeats his compliment from 45:2: the Corinthians know the Scriptures well, so he writes only "to remind" them. The story he chooses is one they would know, Moses on the mountain (Exodus 32).
orig: τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ (ta logia tou theou)

a: your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt
p: Clement follows Moses' own retelling in Deuteronomy 9, in the Greek.
b: Clement's words come from Deuteronomy 9:12-14, Moses' retelling of the golden calf, in the Greek. The site's Deuteronomy, from the Hebrew, reads "Get up and go down from here quickly. Your people whom you brought out of Egypt have ruined themselves" (Deuteronomy 9:12). Clement keeps the Greek "broken the law" and "cast idols," and, from the Greek of Deuteronomy 9:13, the words "I have spoken to you once and twice," which the Hebrew lacks. Where the Greek says God will make Moses a nation "great and strong," Clement has "great and wonderful." The forty days and forty nights of fasting are in Deuteronomy 9:9 and 18. Codices Alexandrinus and Constantinopolitanus add "Moses, Moses" (see the variant).

a: or blot me out too from the book of the living
p: Moses asks to be blotted out with the people. Clement calls it perfect love.
b: In Exodus Moses says, "And now, if you will forgive their sin... But if not, wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32). Clement shortens it into a plain choice: forgive them, or blot me out too. "The book of the living" is the phrase of Psalm 69:28. Paul says something like it of his own people: "I would even wish to be cursed myself, cut off from Christ, on behalf of my brothers" (Romans 9:3). Clement holds Moses up as the model for chapter 54: a leader ready to lose himself so the people may be at peace.

a: The attendant speaks boldly to his Lord.
p: Parrhēsia, free and bold speech, the right of a friend to speak plainly.
b: Parrhēsiazomai is to speak freely, with the boldness of a citizen or a friend. Moses, God's "attendant" (43:1), speaks to God as a friend speaks (Exodus 33:11). The New Testament uses the related noun for the boldness believers have before God through Christ (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19). Clement's wonder ("What great love!") is the hinge to the next chapter.
orig: παρρησιάζεται θεράπων πρὸς κύριον (parrhēsiazetai therapōn pros kyrion)

a: I will step aside. I will go away wherever you want
t: A call to leave for peace
p: Clement asks the leaders of the revolt to leave Corinth for the sake of peace.
b: Clement puts a speech in the mouth of the noble person he hopes is among the rebels: "If the trouble is because of me, I will go." This is the practical heart of the letter. It does not ask the removed elders to leave but those whose rivalry caused the split, so that "Christ's flock" can live at peace with "the elders who have been appointed." Clement then gives examples of such leaving from the history of the nations (55:1). The likeness to Jonah, who said "throw me into the sea" so the storm would stop (Jonah 1:12), is a reader's comparison; Clement does not name him.

a: what the people tell me
p: Plēthos, "the multitude," is the whole assembled church, as in Acts.
b: The Greek is "the things ordered by the multitude." Acts uses the same word for the whole assembled body of believers: the Twelve "called together the whole body of the disciples" (Acts 6:2), and "the whole gathering went quiet" (Acts 15:12). In Clement the people of the church have a real voice: they agreed to their elders' appointment (44:3), and now the departing leader will do what they tell him.
orig: τὰ προστασσόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους (ta prostassomena hypo tou plēthous)

a: the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord
p: Psalm 24:1 in the Greek, the same words as 1 Corinthians 10:26.
b: The words are Psalm 24:1 in the Greek, which Paul also quotes, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's 1 Corinthians 10:26: "For the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord." Paul used the verse to say any food may be eaten; Clement uses it to say that a man who leaves Corinth for peace will find a welcome anywhere, because every place belongs to the Lord.

a: those who live as citizens of God's commonwealth
p: The Greek is political: they "live the citizenship of God."
b: Clement uses the citizen words politeuomai and politeia: "those who conduct as citizens the citizenship of God, which brings no regret." Paul uses the same language: "live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ" (Philippians 1:27) and "we belong to a commonwealth in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). In a Greek city, citizenship came with duties to the common good. Clement's point: a true citizen of God's commonwealth will give up his own place for the peace of all. The Plain English Translation says "commonwealth," as in Philippians 3:20, for the Greek politeia, "citizenship, way of life as a citizen."
orig: οἱ πολιτευόμενοι τὴν ἀμεταμέλητον πολιτείαν τοῦ θεοῦ (hoi politeuomenoi tēn ametamelēton politeian tou theou)

a: Many kings and rulers, when a time of plague came on
p: Clement praises rulers who died for their cities and citizens who left home for peace.
b: Clement now draws "examples from the nations," that is, from outside Israel and the church. He names no one. Lightfoot gives the kind of story he may mean. For rulers and citizens who died for their people, he names the patriotic deeds of Codrus, of Bulis and Sperthias, of Marcus Curtius, of the Decii, and of Menoeceus, who loved Thebes. For men who left their cities to calm faction, he names Lycurgus at Sparta and Scipio Africanus. Origen, as Lightfoot notes, refers to this passage and accepts that such things happened. A Christian letter here holds up non-Christians as models of self-giving. The verdict on the link is simple: Clement borrows the shape of such stories, a life given for the city, not their religion; the oracles they obeyed are mentioned without praise. His real models follow at once, Christians who sold themselves (55:2), and Judith and Esther (55:4-6). Compare John 11:50, where the high priest says unknowingly that one man should die for the people.

a: Many handed themselves over into slavery
p: Some Roman Christians sold themselves as slaves to free others or to feed the poor.
b: Clement says "many among us" gave themselves up to chains to ransom others, and many sold themselves into slavery and fed others with the price. Lightfoot takes "among us" to mean Christians at Rome, and notes that "the ransom of slaves and the support of captives were regarded as a sacred duty by the early Christians generally." The letter offers this as something the Corinthians would believe. Compare Paul, who made himself "a slave to everyone" in a figure (1 Corinthians 9:19), and Hebrews 13:3 on remembering prisoners.

a: The blessed Judith
p: Clement holds up Judith, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and Protestant Bibles do not.
b: Clement calls her "the blessed Judith" and sums up Judith 8-13: when her city was besieged, she asked its elders to let her go out (Judith 8:32-34), went into the enemy camp, and "the Lord has struck him down by a woman's hand" (Judith 13:15; compare Judith 9:10; 16:5). Judith is not in the Hebrew Bible; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it, and Protestant Bibles place it among the Apocrypha or leave it out. Clement uses it as he uses the stories of the Old Testament, as a true example, but he does not introduce it with "it is written." This is an early Christian use of the book (see the site's Judith introduction).

a: by her fasting and her humbling herself
p: Esther's fast is in the Hebrew book; her "humbling" points to the Greek additions.
b: Esther calls the Jews of Susa to fast for three days before she goes to the king (Esther 4:16). Clement's second word, "humbling," points to the Greek form of the book. In Addition C, Esther's prayer, she takes off her royal clothes, covers her head with ashes, and "humbled her body greatly" (in Swete's Greek, set after Esther 4:17). The Additions to Esther are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Clement's title for God, "the all-seeing Master," fits that prayer's "you know all things." His Esther is "perfect in faith," the woman of prayer of the Greek book.

a: with God and the saints
t: Remembered by God and the saints
p: The sinners who yield will be remembered with mercy before God and his holy people.
b: The Greek is literally "the remembrance with mercies toward God and the saints." It may mean that God and the saints (God's holy people, the church) will remember the repentant kindly, or that the church's prayers for them before God will bear fruit. Clement asks the Romans to pray for the rebels, "that forbearance and humility may be given them," and to correct them in love (56:2). The prayer for those who sin is the practice of James 5:16 and 1 John 5:16.
orig: ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ἁγίους μετ᾽ οἰκτιρμῶν μνεία (hē pros ton theon kai tous hagious met' oiktirmōn mneia)

a: The Lord disciplined me hard, but he did not hand me over to death.
p: Clement begins a chain of verses on discipline with Psalm 118:18 in the Greek.
b: The Greek Psalm 118:18 (117:18 there) is "Disciplining, the Lord disciplined me," a doubled verb for force, which the Plain English Translation gives as "disciplined me hard." The site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, reads "Yah has trained me with hard discipline, but to death he did not give me up." Clement goes on to Proverbs 3:12, Psalm 141:5 and Job 5:17-26.

a: For whoever the Lord loves, he disciplines, and he whips every son he takes in.
p: Clement's form matches Hebrews 12:6 exactly, not the Greek Proverbs.
b: Clement quotes Proverbs 3:12 in exactly the form of Hebrews 12:6, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's Hebrews wording. Swete's Greek Proverbs has "rebukes" (elenchei) where Hebrews and Clement have "disciplines" (paideuei). The site's Proverbs, from the Hebrew, reads "For whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes, the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in" (Proverbs 3:12). That Clement agrees with Hebrews against Swete's Greek here fits his use of Hebrews elsewhere (36:2-5).

a: but do not let the oil of sinners anoint my head
p: The Greek Psalm refuses the oil of sinners; the Hebrew welcomes a righteous man's blow as oil.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 141:5 in the Greek (140:5 there): "a righteous man will discipline me in mercy and correct me, but do not let the oil of sinners anoint my head." Clement has the plural "sinners" (hamartōlōn), where Swete's Greek Psalm has the singular, "a sinner" (hamartōlou). The Hebrew reads differently, in the site's wording: "If a righteous man hits me, it is loyal love; if he scolds me, it is oil on my head, and my head will not refuse it." In the Hebrew the correction itself is the oil; in the Greek the oil belongs to sinners and is refused. Clement's point fits the Greek: take correction from the righteous, not flattery from sinners.

a: Blessed is the man the Lord has corrected.
p: Clement quotes Eliphaz's speech in the Greek, verse by verse.
b: Verses 56:6-15 are Job 5:17-26 in the Greek, which Clement follows almost word for word. The Hebrew, in the site's wording, begins "Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him! So do not spurn the Almighty's discipline" (Job 5:17). Clement uses the words as Scripture ("it says"), though in Job they belong to Eliphaz, one of the friends whom God later says did not speak rightly (Job 42:7). Paul also quotes Eliphaz as Scripture (Job 5:13 in 1 Corinthians 3:19). The promise is of protection for the one who accepts God's discipline.

a: like ripe grain harvested in its season
p: Job 5:26: death in old age, like a harvest gathered in.
b: This is the last line of Eliphaz's promise, Job 5:26, in the Greek. The site's Job, from the Hebrew, reads "Still strong, you will go down to your tomb, as a stack of sheaves goes up at harvest time." Death at the right time, after a full life, is a blessing; Clement has already called the elders who died before the trouble "blessed," whose "departure was fruitful and complete" (44:5).

a: For he is a good Father
p: God disciplines as a good father, so that we may be shown mercy.
b: Clement sums up the chain of verses as Hebrews 12:7-11 does: God treats us as sons, and discipline is for our good. "We had the fathers of our flesh to discipline us, and we showed them respect. Will we not much more put ourselves under the Father of spirits, and live?" (Hebrews 12:9). Clement calls God "the Master of spirits" in 64:1.

a: bending the knees of your heart
p: A picture of inner humility, as in the Prayer of Manasseh.
b: To kneel was the posture of prayer and of surrender. Clement asks the rebels to bend the knees of their heart, that is, to humble themselves inwardly. The Prayer of Manasseh has the same picture: "Now I bend my heart's knee" (Prayer of Manasseh 11). Whether Clement knew that prayer or both used a common way of speaking cannot be shown. "Submit to the elders" is the command of 1 Peter 5:5: "you younger ones, submit yourselves to the elders."
r: Prayer of Manasseh 11; 1 Peter 5:5; Ephesians 3:14; Hebrews 13:17

a: the all-excellent Wisdom
p: A title of the book of Proverbs among the early Christians.
b: Hē panaretos sophia, "Wisdom of every virtue," names the speaker of Proverbs 1, Wisdom herself, and it was also a title of the book. Eusebius reports that Hegesippus, "and not only he, but also Irenæus and the whole company of the ancients, called the Proverbs of Solomon All-virtuous Wisdom" (Church History 4.22). Clement quotes Proverbs 1:23-33 in the Greek in 57:3-7.
orig: ἡ πανάρετος σοφία (hē panaretos sophia)

a: did not choose the fear of the Lord
p: Clement quotes Proverbs 1:23-33 in the Greek, which differs from the Hebrew at many points.
b: Verses 57:3-7 are Proverbs 1:23-33 in the Greek. Clement follows it closely, with small changes. At 57:5 he has "the fear of the Lord," as the Hebrew does (Proverbs 1:29), where Swete's Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has "the word of the Lord." At 57:4 he leaves out the Greek's last line of Proverbs 1:27 ("or when destruction comes on you"). The Greek of Proverbs 1:23 ("I will pour out to you a saying from my breath") is far from the Hebrew's "I will pour out my spirit," and the Greek of 1:32 ("because they wronged the simple") is far from the Hebrew, where the simple are not wronged but undone by their own turning away ("Turning away is what kills the naive," Proverbs 1:32). The Greek nēpioi, "infants, the simple," stands for the same Hebrew word. The site's Proverbs follows the Hebrew.

a: But whoever listens to me will make his home in hope
p: From 57:7 to the end of chapter 63 the older Greek manuscript is lost. The Greek rests on one manuscript of 1056.
b: Lake's footnote: "A is missing from here to the beginning of Chapter LXIV." Lightfoot gives the exact place: a leaf of Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD) "has disappeared," so that it "omits from § 57 ἀνθ᾽ ὧν γὰρ ἠδίκουν [57:7, 'because they wronged'] to the end of § 63." So for 57:7, for 58-63 and for the great prayer, the Greek text rests on a single Greek manuscript, the Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, copied in 1056), checked against the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions and the quotations of Clement of Alexandria. Lake judges that the witnesses vary little.

a: For as God lives
t: An oath by God, Christ and the Spirit
p: Clement swears by the living God, Christ and the Spirit, the Old Testament oath made threefold.
b: In the Old Testament the solemn oath is "As the LORD lives" (Judges 8:19; 1 Samuel 14:39). Clement makes it threefold: God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, whom he calls together "the faith and the hope of the chosen." The three are named side by side as in Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14, and as in 46:6 ("one God ... one Christ, and one Spirit"). Clement does not explain how the three relate; he names them together as the ground of the church's faith. On the repeated "lives," see the variant.

a: enrolled and counted in the number of those who are saved
p: A roll-call picture: names entered on the list of the saved, which 59:2 asks God to keep whole.
b: The words are those of a city roll: "enrolled" (put in the ranks) and "counted" (reckoned, held in esteem). The prayer that follows asks God to keep "the counted number of his chosen" unbroken (59:2). The picture is the book of life (53:4; Revelation 3:5; Luke 10:20). For Clement the saved are known to God by number, and the one who keeps God's commands in humility is on the list.
orig: ἐντεταγμένος καὶ ἐλλόγιμος ἔσται εἰς τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν σωζομένων (entetagmenos kai ellogimos estai eis ton arithmon tōn sōzomenōn)

a: glory to him
p: The Greek says "to him," without naming God or Christ.
b: The Greek is di' hou estin autō hē doxa, "through whom is the glory to him." "Through him" is Jesus Christ, named just before. "To him" can point back to God, whose "decrees and commands" are named in the same sentence, or to Christ; the Greek does not name him, so the Plain English Translation keeps "him," as Lake's English does. The same form closes 64:1 and 65:2; 61:3 says "to you," and 50:7 and 45:7 give glory "to him" with Christ or God as the nearest name.
orig: δι᾽ οὗ ἐστὶν αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα (di' hou estin autō hē doxa)

a: what God has said through us
p: Clement says God speaks "through us." What authority does the Roman church claim here?
b: Clement says the letter's words are spoken "by him through us," and in 63:2 that it was written "through the Holy Spirit." Irenaeus later wrote that "the Church in Rome dispatched a most powerful letter to the Corinthians, exhorting them to peace" (Against Heresies 3.3.3). The 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia reads it this way: "Clement evidently writes officially, with all that authority of the Roman Church," while noting that "no appeal seems to have been made to Rome." Lake stresses that the letter "clearly claims to be not the letter of a single person but of a church." The letter itself speaks throughout as "we," the church, names no bishop of Rome or of Corinth, and rests its appeal on Scripture, the apostles and the Holy Spirit (63:2). Whether Peter's successors lead the church is the card at Matthew 16:18.

a: his beloved servant Jesus Christ
p: Pais means both servant and child. The site says "servant," as in the prayers of Acts.
b: Greek pais can mean "child" or "servant." Lake translates "his beloved child." The Greek Isaiah calls God's chosen one "my servant" with this word (ho pais mou, Isaiah 42:1; 52:13), and Matthew 12:18 quotes Isaiah 42:1 with "my beloved." The prayers of the first church use it of Jesus beside "your servant David" (Acts 4:25, 27, 30; compare Acts 3:13, "his servant Jesus"). Lightfoot agrees that in Isaiah the word is "servant, minister," but adds that "the higher sense of υἱός [son] was soon imported into the ambiguous word παῖς," citing the Apostolic Constitutions and Irenaeus, and that "so Clement seems to have used the word here." His own English has "Son." The site keeps "servant" in 59:2, 59:3 and 59:4, because the prayer's pairing follows the prayers of Acts and the Greek Isaiah. "Beloved" is the Father's word at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:11).
orig: διὰ τοῦ ἠγαπημένου παιδὸς αὐτοῦ (dia tou ēgapēmenou paidos autou)
r: Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 52:13; Matthew 12:18; Acts 3:13; Acts 4:25-30; Mark 1:11

a: from darkness into light
p: The calling from darkness to light, as in Acts 26:18 and 1 Peter 2:9.
b: The risen Jesus sent Paul "to open their eyes, so they turn back from darkness to light" (Acts 26:18), and 1 Peter 2:9 speaks of "the one who called you out of darkness into his astonishing light." Clement adds a second pair, "from not knowing into knowing," with epignōsis, full knowledge, the word of Colossians 1:9-10.

a: the eyes of our heart
p: The praise of 59:3 is almost all Old Testament phrases, joined in a chain.
b: The prayer begins with Ephesians 1:18 ("May the eyes of your heart be lit up") and then praises God in phrases from the Old Testament, as Lake's margin notes. God dwells on high and with the lowly (Isaiah 57:15); humbles the insolence of the proud (Isaiah 13:11); lifts the lowly and brings the lofty low (Job 5:11; Luke 1:52, "raised the lowly high"); "makes people poor and makes them rich" and "kills and makes alive" (1 Samuel 2:6-7; Deuteronomy 32:39); and is "God of the spirits of all flesh" (Numbers 16:22; 27:16). Clement prays in the language of Hannah's and Mary's songs.
r: Ephesians 1:18; Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 13:11; Job 5:11; 1 Samuel 2:6-8; Deuteronomy 32:39; Luke 1:51-53; Numbers 16:22; Numbers 27:16

a: the Maker and the Overseer of every spirit
p: The word for church "overseers" is here used of God himself.
b: God is "the Maker and Overseer (episkopos) of every spirit." It is the word the letter uses for the church's overseers (42:4-5), and 1 Peter 2:25 uses it of Christ: "the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls." Clement's readers would hear that the human overseers share a title of God, who watches over all.
orig: τὸν παντὸς πνεύματος κτίστην καὶ ἐπίσκοπον (ton pantos pneumatos ktistēn kai episkopon)

a: Lift the fallen to their feet.
p: The petitions echo Psalm 146 and the Jewish daily prayer that praises God who lifts the fallen.
b: The list of petitions (save, have mercy, lift the fallen, heal the sick, ransom the prisoners, feed the hungry) gathers the acts of God praised in Psalm 146:7-8: "who hands bread to the hungry. The LORD unties the prisoners" and "raises those bent double." The same acts stand in the second blessing of the Amidah, the Jewish standing prayer said every day: God is somekh noflim ve-rofe cholim u-matir asurim, "who holds up the fallen, heals the sick and sets free the bound," and memit u-mechayeh, "who puts to death and gives life" (the siddur's Hebrew on Sefaria). The exact first-century wording of the Amidah is not known, so the likeness shows a shared Jewish way of praying more than borrowing. Lightfoot looks forward, to later Christian prayers that drew on this one, such as the Apostolic Constitutions, book 8.
orig: τοὺς πεπτωκότας ἔγειρον ... τοὺς ἀσθενεῖς ἴασαι ... λύτρωσαι τοὺς δεσμίους ἡμῶν

a: that we are your people, the sheep of your pasture
p: The prayer ends with Solomon's prayer and Psalm 100: let all nations know who God is.
b: The closing lines echo Solomon: "so that every people on earth will know that the LORD is God. There is no other" (1 Kings 8:60; compare 2 Kings 19:19) and Psalm 100:3 ("his people, the flock he pastures"; compare Psalm 79:13). Clement adds one line no Old Testament prayer has: that Jesus Christ is God's servant. The prayer for "all the nations" fits a church in the capital of an empire of many peoples.

a: the everlasting order of the world
t: The everlasting frame of the world
p: Systasis is the structure that holds the world together.
b: Systasis means the standing-together, the frame or structure of a thing. Clement praised the ordered working of the cosmos in chapter 20. Here he says that God made that order "plain to see" through what he does in it, much as Paul says God's power is seen in what he made (Romans 1:20). The word for "inhabited world," oikoumenē, is the one used for the Roman world (Luke 2:1).
orig: τὴν ἀέναον τοῦ κόσμου σύστασιν (tēn aenaon tou kosmou systasin)

a: Merciful and compassionate one
p: The old confession of God's character, from Exodus 34 through Joel.
b: The pair goes back to God's self-description to Moses (Exodus 34:6) and is repeated through the Old Testament: "he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love" (Joel 2:13; compare 2 Chronicles 30:9; Jonah 4:2). Sirach 2:11 has "The Lord is full of pity and mercy; he forgives sins." The prayer then asks for that forgiveness, using four words for sin: lawless acts, wrongs, failings, faults.

a: before you and before our rulers
p: The church prays to do good in the sight of God and of the Roman authorities.
b: Deuteronomy speaks of doing what is good and right in the eyes of the LORD (Deuteronomy 12:28). Clement adds "and before our rulers." Paul and Peter likewise ask believers to do good so that rulers have no just complaint (Romans 13:3; 1 Peter 2:14-15). The prayer does not make the church simply content with Rome: the same prayer asks to be rescued "from those who hate us without cause" (60:3), and it comes from the church whose apostles had been killed (5:4-7).

a: let your face shine on us for good, in peace
p: The words of Aaron's blessing, and the "strong hand" and "high arm" of the Exodus.
b: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25) was the blessing the priests spoke over Israel, and the Psalms pray it back to God (Psalm 67:1; 80:3, 7, 19). The strong hand and high arm are the words for God's rescue from Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:34; 5:15; Jeremiah 32:21). Clement asks for a new rescue, from sin and from enemies.
r: Numbers 6:24-26; Psalm 67:1; Psalm 80:3; Deuteronomy 4:34; Deuteronomy 5:15; Psalm 35:19

a: Make us obedient to your almighty and glorious name, and to our rulers
p: The Greek has a participle that could describe "us" or "our fathers."
b: The Greek runs on: "as you gave to our fathers ... becoming obedient to your almighty and glorious name and to our rulers." The participle can be read with "us" (give us peace as we become obedient), which Lake and the Plain English Translation follow, or with "our fathers" (who obeyed God and their rulers). Either way, obedience to God and to rulers stand side by side, and chapter 61 explains why: God gave the rulers their power.
orig: ὑπηκόους γινομένους τῷ παντοκράτορι καὶ ἐνδόξῳ ὀνόματί σου (hypēkoous ginomenous tō pantokratori kai endoxō onomati sou)

a: You, Master, gave them the authority of kingship
p: The church prays for the rulers whose power comes from God, perhaps under a persecuting emperor.
b: Clement prays that God give the rulers "health, peace, harmony and steadiness." He grounds obedience in God's gift of their power, as Paul does: "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1). The church obeys 1 Timothy 2:1-2: "make requests ... for kings and for all who hold high office, so that we can spend calm and quiet lives." If the letter dates from Domitian's time, as Lake allows, the church is praying for an emperor under whom it may have suffered, though Lake notes "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian." Lightfoot sets this prayer beside Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2. When Christians may resist rulers is on the card at Romans 13:1.
r: Romans 13:1-7; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Titus 3:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Jeremiah 29:7; Acts 5:29

a: King of the ages
p: Over the earthly rulers stands the King of the ages, who gives them their glory.
b: The prayer for the rulers is framed by God's greater kingship: "To the King of the ages, who cannot decay and cannot be seen, the only God: honor and glory to him forever and ever" (1 Timothy 1:17; compare Tobit 13:6, "lift high the King of the ages"). Human rulers have "glory and honor and authority" only because he gives it (Daniel 2:21, 37). Clement asks that they rule "in peace and gentleness, in a godly way," and so find God's mercy: a prayer for the rulers' own good, not only the church's.
r: 1 Timothy 1:17; Tobit 13:6; Revelation 15:3; Daniel 2:21; Daniel 2:37; Psalm 8:5-6

a: the high priest and protector of our souls, Jesus Christ
p: Clement's title for Christ, here and in 64:1, joins Hebrews and 1 Peter.
b: Clement has called Christ "the high priest of our offerings" (36:1), as Hebrews calls him "the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus" (Hebrews 3:1). Prostatēs is a patron, a protector who stands before others and speaks for them. 1 Peter 2:25 calls Christ "the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls." Through this high priest the church brings its thanks, exomologoumetha (see the note at 52:1).
orig: διὰ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως καὶ προστάτου τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν (dia tou archiereōs kai prostatou tōn psychōn hēmōn)

a: faith and repentance, real love, self-control, self-restraint and endurance
p: Clement lists the subjects he has covered, a guide to the whole letter.
b: Clement reviews his letter: faith (9-12; 31-32), repentance (7-8), love (49-50), endurance (5; 45), harmony and peace (19-21; 60-61), and humility after the example of "our fathers" (13-19). The words "self-control" (enkrateia) and "self-restraint" (sōphrosynē) were virtues of the good citizen in Greek ethics, and Clement asks for them again in the closing blessing (64:1). The whole letter has been an appeal for harmony (Greek homonoia), the word that returns in 63:2 and 65:1.

a: to bow our necks
p: The picture of an ox taking the yoke: submission.
b: Literally "to put the neck under." The picture is of an ox bowing to the yoke. Jeremiah used it of submission to Babylon ("the nation that brings its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon," Jeremiah 27:11), and Sirach of learning wisdom (Sirach 51:26). Jesus offered his own yoke (Matthew 11:29). Clement includes the Romans ("our") and asks all to take their "place in obedience" and end the "empty rebellion."

a: what we have written through the Holy Spirit
p: Clement claims the Spirit's guidance for his letter, but not the standing of Scripture.
b: Clement says the letter was written "through the Holy Spirit." He claims the same for Paul (47:3) and for the Scriptures (45:2), yet he uses "it is written" only for the Old Testament. The claim shows how a church leader of his time understood guidance by the Spirit, not that he was writing new Scripture. Some early churches did read the letter aloud in worship: Eusebius says it "has been publicly used in a great many churches both in former times and in our own" (Church History 3.16), and he quotes the bishop of Corinth, writing to Rome about AD 170, that his church had read a Roman letter on "the Lord's holy day" (4.23.11). No church counts it as Scripture today.

a: They will be witnesses between you and us.
p: Rome sends trusted older men who will carry the letter and report back.
b: The letter is carried by men "who have lived among us without blame from youth to old age," named in 65:1. They are to be "witnesses between you and us," that is, to see how Corinth responds and to report it. Letters in the ancient world were carried by trusted messengers who could explain them, as Tychicus carried Paul's letters (Colossians 4:7-8; Ephesians 6:21-22). If these men had been Christians from their youth, the Roman church had members who had believed for decades.

a: the Master of spirits and Lord of all flesh
p: A title from Numbers 16:22 and 27:16, "the God of the spirits of all flesh."
b: Moses and Aaron prayed to "God, God of the spirits of all flesh" (Numbers 16:22; compare Numbers 27:16), and Hebrews calls God "the Father of spirits" (Hebrews 12:9). Clement splits the old title in two: "Master of spirits and Lord of all flesh." The blessing asks God to give every believer the virtues of 62:2. Here Codex Alexandrinus resumes after its lost page (see the note at 57:7).

a: a people that is his own private treasure
p: The title of Israel in Deuteronomy, given to the church as in Titus 2:14.
b: The Greek laos periousios is the Septuagint's phrase for Israel: "The LORD has chosen you to be a people that is his own private treasure, out of all the peoples on the face of the earth" (Deuteronomy 14:2; compare Exodus 19:5). Titus 2:14 gives the title to the church: "a people that is his own private treasure, eager for good works." Clement adds that God first "chose the Lord Jesus Christ," and chose believers "through him." Whether such titles mean the church replaces Israel or shares in its calling is on the cards at Galatians 6:16 and Acts 28.
orig: εἰς λαὸν περιούσιον (eis laon periousion)

a: Claudius Ephebus and Valerius Bito, with Fortunatus too
p: The names may point to men of the imperial household.
b: Claudius and Valerius are Roman family names. Lightfoot notes that they "suggest some connexion with the imperial household; as the fifth Cæsar with his two predecessors belonged to the Claudian gens and his empress Messalina to the Valerian," and judges it "fairly probable that they are in some way connected with the palace," like "those from Caesar's household" who greet the Philippians (Philippians 4:22). Fortunatus may not be one of them: Lightfoot says the wording "seems to separate Fortunatus from Ephebus and Bito," so that he was "perhaps not a Roman who accompanied the letter, but a Corinthian from whom Clement was expecting a visit." In that case he sees "no improbability" in identifying him with the Fortunatus who visited Paul from Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:17), though "Fortunatus is a very common name."

a: The letter of the Romans to the Corinthians.
p: The old title names the church of Rome as the sender, not Clement.
b: The closing title in Lake's Greek is "Letter of the Romans to the Corinthians." The letter itself never names Clement, and Lake notes that it "clearly claims to be not the letter of a single person but of a church." The name of Clement comes from tradition: Eusebius says he "wrote it in the name of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth" (Church History 3.16). The site's introduction to the book sets out the evidence for Clement as author.
